content: 1. The frequency of consuming green leafy and orange vegetables was not associated with wasting, underweight status, or stunting in children. Measurements were conducted using recumbent length to the nearest millimeter by trained staff, with follow-up assessments performed seven months later. Age was determined through interviews with the infant's mother. 2. The certainty of evidence regarding the impact of vegetable consumption on height-for-age Z-scores was rated as very low. This was due to the limited data available, inconsistencies in findings, and imprecision in measurements. A trend was observed suggesting lower height-for-age Z-scores with less frequent vegetable consumption, but the evidence was insufficient to draw definitive conclusions. 3. Serum ferritin levels (<20 μg/L) were assessed using venous blood samples collected before 12 a.m., with hematological tests performed within six hours. The results indicated no significant relationship between the frequency of vegetable consumption and the likelihood of having very low iron stores (ferritin <15 μg/L). However, the findings were inconsistent, as the negative effect of consuming vegetables once per day was not observed in those consuming vegetables more frequently. 4. Anemia prevalence was not associated with the consumption of dark green vegetables. Hemoglobin levels were measured using capillary blood samples obtained through heel or finger puncture, with a hemoglobin concentration of <11 g/dL used as the diagnostic threshold for anemia. Approximately 2% of children who consumed dark green vegetables in the past 24 hours did not have anemia. 5. A cross-sectional study conducted in Aceh, Indonesia, included 392 healthy children aged 6–23 months. The study assessed complementary feeding practices and nutritional status. Data on the frequency of fruit, vegetable, animal-source food, and non-plant-source food consumption were collected through repeated 24-hour recalls. Vegetable consumption frequency was categorized as ≥4 times per week, 1–3 times per week, or never. 6. The study in rural Senegal included 543 children aged 6–42 months as part of the Intermittent Preventive Malaria Treatment trial. Measurements of height and weight were taken in September 2002 and again seven months later. Caregivers provided information on the frequency of fruit and vegetable consumption through 24-hour recalls. Frequency was defined as 0–2 days per week or ≥3 days per week. The study did not adjust for confounding variables, and the certainty of evidence was downgraded due to imprecision and a small sample size. 7. A cross-sectional study in Norway included 74 healthy infants aged 1 year. Dietary intake was assessed using a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) based on pilot study results. Frequency of fruit and vegetable consumption was categorized as several times per day, once per day, or less than once per day. The study lacked sufficient methodological detail, making it challenging to evaluate internal validity. The small sample size and lack of adjustment for confounding variables further limited the reliability of the findings. 8. A longitudinal cohort study in Norway followed 9,025 mother-infant pairs over five years, with dietary intake assessed at 18 months, 36 months, and 7 years of age. Frequency of fruit and vegetable consumption was categorized as low, medium, or high. The study lacked confidence intervals and did not account for confounding variables, leading to a very low certainty rating for the evidence. 9. The frequency of fruit consumption was not associated with wasting, underweight status, or stunting in children. Measurements were conducted using recumbent length and standing height, with follow-up assessments performed seven months later. Age was determined through interviews with the infant's mother. 10. Overall, the studies reviewed had significant limitations, including small sample sizes, lack of adjustment for confounding variables, and insufficient methodological detail. Many studies were cross-sectional in design, limiting the ability to establish causality. The certainty of evidence for most outcomes was rated as very low due to imprecision, inconsistency, and risk of bias.
